newsitem.title: USA: House rejects term limits amendments.
newsitem.headline: House rejects term limits amendments.

text.p: The House of Representatives on Wednesday rejected all 11 versions of a constitutional amendment to set congressional term limits as supporters disagreed over which one to back.

The amendments would have limited House members to three, four or six two-year terms and senators to two six-year terms. One would have applied term limits retroactively to current members while another would let states set shorter limits if they wished.

Only the last amendment to set 12-year limits for members of both chambers got even more than half the votes. The 217-211 result was 69 votes short of the required two-thirds majority. A similar amendment got 227 votes two years ago.
A constitutional amendment must get a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress plus ratification by three-quarters of the 50 states in order to become law.

Widespread differences in Congress on how to approach a very delicate political issue -- popular with many voters but touchy among lawmakers, whose careers could be jeopardised -- guaranteed that the term-limits drive would fall short again.
"If I had wanted to develop a strategy to blow up the term limits efforts, I would have developed that strategy," House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas told reporters.

The issue has widespread support among Republican conservatives and was part of their Contract with America, a list of campaign promises that underpinned their 1994 congressional election victories. But Armey said term limits backers must agree on a single amendment in order to have a chance of winning.

Some states had passed term-limits laws restricting their own representatives and senators, but the Supreme Court has thrown them out and ruled that the only way to set such limits was to amend the Constitution.

So strong is term-limit support in some areas that nine states have passed laws requiring their members of Congress to vote for a specific version of term limits or have a label placed by their names on the next election ballot stating "disregarded voter instructions on term limits."

Despite the defeats, some term limit supporters said the votes were worthwhile because they put members on record and increased pressure on opponents to change their position or risk defeat in the next election.

"Term limits is the best reform we could bring to Congress," said Representative Bob Inglis, a South Carolina Republican. He said it would make Congress more responsive to voters by forcing out career lawmakers who gain power through seniority.
But opponents said it would force out experienced members.
"This is no place for amateurs," said Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican and 22-year veteran of the House.

"The framers of the Constitution knew that the best way to ensure representative democracy is to make members of Congress constantly accountable to the voters," added Representative John Conyers, a Michigan Democrat who has served 32 years.
"The system works to give us new blood," said Texas Republican Tom DeLay. He said more than half of the current House members had served three terms or less.
The U.S. Constitution sets House terms at two years and Senate terms at six years, but has no limit on how many times members may run for re-election.
Presidents have been limited to two four year terms since ratification of an amendment in 1951 and 41 states have term limits for their governors and other state officials.
